name: Feedback Students Actually Use
title: Feedback Students Actually Use
answer: Feedback Students Actually Use is the idea that AI writing feedback only counts when students act on it. The book reports that AI feedback can improve revisions and motivation, yet nearly half of more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12 changed nothing after receiving it. The design that works ties feedback to the class rubric and makes revision part of the assignment, with the teacher reading the final version and assigning the grade.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: Writing feedback is described in this volume as one of the strongest uses of AI. The problem it solves is that good feedback on its own accomplishes nothing if the student never returns to the draft. The fix is a cycle rather than a comment: a student submits a draft, receives feedback aimed at specific rubric points, revises the work, and explains what was changed. The teacher then reads the final version and assigns the grade, so the feedback is bound to the assignment instead of sitting beside it. Figure 6.3 shows this cycle.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text sets out one cycle rather than separate routines for each grade band, though the research it cites covers students in grades 1 through 12 and tenth graders writing in English as a foreign language. In that cycle a student submits a draft, receives feedback on specific rubric points, revises, and explains what they changed. The teacher reads the final version and assigns the grade. Teachers can also see who actually revised, because Google Docs version history shows every change a student made and when. Tracking this for a few weeks often surprises teachers, and it gives them a clear, fair basis for conversations with students who are not revising.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a formal evidence label to this idea, but it calls writing feedback one of the strongest uses of AI in this volume and cites research for it. In a randomized trial with 459 tenth graders writing in English as a foreign language, feedback from an AI model improved the quality of their revisions and raised their motivation for future writing (Meyer et al., 2023). A later trial found no clear difference in revision quality between teacher feedback and AI feedback, though teacher feedback may have carried over slightly better to the next task (Meyer et al., 2026). A review of 20 studies found a medium effect of automated writing feedback overall (Fleckenstein et al., 2023). When researchers compared feedback side by side, trained teachers still wrote better feedback than an AI in most categories (Steiss et al., 2024).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets out two cautions alongside the promise. When researchers compared feedback side by side, trained teachers still wrote better feedback than an AI in most categories (Steiss et al., 2024). Across more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12, nearly half did not change a single character after receiving AI feedback (Jansen et al., 2025). Feedback that is not acted on does nothing, however good it is. The teacher reads the final version and assigns the grade, so the grading decision stays with a person, and tracking revision gives a clear, fair basis for conversations with students who are not revising.
